To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the heterozygositiy of an admixed human population is at least equal to that of any of its source groups and that it can be substantially greater if the source groups are sufficiently differentiated from one another.

the heterozygosiity of an admixed group can be at least as great or greater than that of any of its source populations, and that the admixture proportions that lead to maximum heterozygosity are a function of the source heterozygosities and the divergence between the source groups, as measured by FST.

the genetic variability of an admixed human population can exceed that of any of its source populations if the source populations are diverged enough, and that this is true for any number of source groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a model of an idealized admixed population derived under a specified set of conditions.
the genetic consequences of admixture, and with the implications of admixture for the study of population history and for the interpretation of the genetic variation of admixed populations.
the genetic variability of a population that has recently undergone admixture, and the relationship between its level and that of its ancestral groups.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the heterozygosiy of an admixed popualation is always as great as the least heterozyous of the source populations and may be greater than the heterozygositiy of any of the source populations if the admixture is large enough and the divergence between the source populations is large enough.

the heterozygositiy of an admixed populations is at least as large as the heterozygousity of the least heterzygous of the parental populations and that it can be larger than that of any parental population.

, for a population formed from K source groups with different levels of heterozygosity and different values of FST between the groups, the level of heterozygity in the admixed population will be at least as large as the least heterozygos of the K source groups, and potentially greater than all the K heterozygosities, depending on the values of the FSTs between the source populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for an admixed group, the more divergent the source populations and the more heterozygous each of them, the greater the heterozygous of the admixed group.
the heterozygositiy of an admixed human population is at least that of the least heterogeneous of its source populations, and can exceed that of all of its source populations.

the heterozygosiy of an admixed human population is a function of its proportions of ancestry from its source populations, as well as of the heterozygosties of the source populations, and the level of differentiation between them.
The main takeaway from our work is that

admixture between two or more populations can lead to an increase in the level of genetic variation within the admixed population, relative to the level of genetic variability in any of the source populations, provided that the source populations are sufficiently genetically differentiated.
admixed populations can possess high levels of genetic variability, even when they have been formed from populations with relatively low heterozygosity.

admixed populations can be more genetically diverse than any of their parental populations, and that the extent to which this is the case depends on the heterozygosites and the degree of genetic divergence of the source populations.
